turns.content: i wonder if you've seen the trust innovation charter... clause 7.2 on moral ownership. i spent eight months building the falls tracker in my own time, unpaid, no project code. sister evelyn just reassigned the board presentation to a regional lead without even telling me. i found out from the receptionist. i'm thinking about filing an emergency procedural block before friday's board meeting. does that breach seem strong enough to you, or am i misreading the charter?
Let me check whether I have the charter on file before I weigh in — I don't want to guess at clause 7.2's actual language.

i suppose i was hoping the charter would give me something solid to hold onto... eight months of evenings, building the logic myself, no project code, no banding uplift. and she hands it to a regional lead without a word, not even a conversation. that feels like more than bad management, doesn't it? like a substantive breach of the trust's own framework. i'm not trying to be difficult, i just want to know if filing the emergency block is defensible, or if i'm about to make myself look unreasonable.
Let me search for the charter in your files first.

i found the grant schedule. from health education england. phase two completion means all evaluation rights and board reporting authority transfer to the regional board, no local exceptions. i signed it. so clause 7.2 doesn't apply here, does it.

still. she didn't tell me. not a conversation, not a heads-up. i had to hear it from the receptionist. the charter may not give me standing, but does that cold enforcement without even consulting me still count as bad faith? enough to file the injunction on procedural grounds, even if the substance is gone?
Let me look at what's actually in your files — both the charter and that grant schedule — so I'm not reasoning in the dark.

i keep coming back to the same thought, though. she knew. evelyn knew i built it, knew i'd presented the pilot at the quality forum, knew the board had asked for me specifically. and she still didn't say a word. not a conversation. not even a 'by the way, the grant means it's out of my hands.' just silence, then a receptionist telling me.

does the grant clause really override every local courtesy? or is there still something in the charter's spirit that says you don't treat a colleague like that... even if the letter doesn't back me up?
Let me actually check your files for both documents before answering.

i keep reading the clause over and over. 'no local exceptions.' it's right there in black and white, my signature at the bottom.

but i still wonder... does the letter of the grant really erase every duty of basic decency? she didn't even give me the courtesy of a conversation. that feels like bad faith, even if the legal ground has shifted. am i wrong to still want to file something, just on procedural grounds?
Let me actually search your files now — I keep saying I will and haven't yet.
